interest: This document provides valuable insight into pre-World War II Japanese soft-power diplomacy and commercial infiltration in Latin America through educational exchange and technical assistance. It demonstrates how Japan utilized scholarships in specialized fields like fisheries to cultivate goodwill and establish footholds in Mexico, prompting close surveillance by U.S. Ambassador Josephus Daniels amidst escalating tensions in the Far East. Furthermore, the cross-reference to file 812.628/540 illustrates the intersection of cultural relations, economic intelligence, and national security in State Department recordkeeping.
overview: This file contains a single 'List of Papers' docket sheet (Sheet 1) for State Department decimal file 894.42712, titled 'Cultural relations between Japan and Mexico. Exchange of professors and students. Attendance of Mexican students in schools of Japan.' The sheet records a single entry from June 19, 1939, originating from U.S. Ambassador Josephus Daniels in Mexico, which outlines Japanese efforts to entrench themselves in Mexican fisheries. The entry summarizes past Japanese initiatives providing technical experts and scholarships to three Mexican students (two of whom later worked in the Mexican Fisheries Department), notes a pending offer to sponsor another Mexican student in Japan free of charge, predicts increased Japanese overtures due to critical conditions in the Far East, and cross-references file 812.628/540.

subfiles.about: A State Department List of Papers docket sheet summarizing a June 19, 1939 despatch from Ambassador Daniels on Japanese scholarships and fisheries influence in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: This List of Papers docket sheet registers an incoming report dated June 19, 1939, from Ambassador Josephus Daniels in Mexico regarding Japanese efforts to establish influence in Mexican fisheries. The entry details Japan's past provision of technical experts and scholarships for three Mexican students, two of whom subsequently joined the Mexican Fisheries Department. It also reports a pending Japanese offer to fund the training of at least one additional Mexican student in Japan, noting that Japanese outreach was likely to expand in light of critical developments in the Far East. The document concludes with a cross-reference directing researchers to file 812.628/540.
subfiles.title: List of Papers: Cultural Relations Between Japan and Mexico
